text: Inflammation is the body's protective response to infection, injury, or irritation, meant to contain the problem — it is a process, not a disease, and should normally be short-lived. External-organ inflammation (e.g. arthritis in a joint) shows as redness, swelling, pain, and local heat. Treatment becomes worthwhile when inflammation persists or causes significant pain or dysfunction — for example, in mastitis, a swollen, hot, hard udder causes real discomfort (the animal stops eating, resists her young approaching the teats); an anti-inflammatory injection reduces heat and swelling, making the udder supple again and letting antibiotics work better on the infected tissue. Two categories exist: steroidal (e.g. Cortisone, Prednisolone, Dexamethasone), with a strong anti-inflammatory effect — Dexamethasone is often combined with antibiotics for respiratory infections, since treating the inflammation (coughing from inflamed bronchi/lungs) helps the antibiotic work and the animal recover better; and non-steroidal (e.g. Aspirin, Paracetamol, Analgin), with a weaker anti-inflammatory effect but a clear benefit for pain and fever.
